sources.note: Nothing; cites only Blench 2006 wordlist, Blench 2004, Atlas 2019.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2020. Research on the Plateau languages of Central Nigeria. Afrika und Übersee 93: 3-44. DOI 10.15460/auue.2020.93.1.209.
sources.note: Nothing on Yangkam phonology. Sec. 2.1 Tarokoid pp. 17-18: classification; 'Of the Tarokoid languages, only Tarok itself is beginning to have an acceptable level of documentation.. Yaŋkam is severely threatened and should be subject to an intensive investigation while speakers are still fluent.'

sources.citation: Longtau, Selbut R. 2016 [2014]. A comparative morphology of non-productive Tarok affixes and stems for suggested Proto-Tarokoid reconstruction of some lexemes. Paper for 'Towards Proto-Niger-Congo' 2, Paris: LLACAN.
sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 2.4 + Table 7 compare Yangkam stems with Tarok affixes; fn.: 'only tones of Tarok examples may be regarded to have been marked accurately'. No stress statement for any Tarokoid language.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2006. The Yangkam language of Central Nigeria and its affinities. Draft circulated for comment (printout April 25, 2006). Cambridge: Mallam Dendo. ii+17 pp. [Internet Archive copy 20130418 of rogerblench.info; identical digest in all captures 2013-2025]
sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 3 Phonology (p. 4) = 3.1 vowels (seven), 3.2 consonants, 3.3 Tones: 'The tone system of Yangkam is quite restricted, with only two tones. The majority of words appear all low tone. No cases of glide tones seem to occur.' Intro p. 2: 'In general, tones are not marked'. No occurrence of stress/accent/syllable/prosody anywhere in the 19 pp.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2004. Tarok and related languages of East-Central Nigeria: nomenclature and subclassification. Circulation draft, printout 22 Oct 2004, 21 pp. (Glottolog 80840).
sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 2.3 Yangkam = nomenclature/location/status; 3.3 Phonology = proto-Tarokoid vowel and consonant correspondences; p. 12 'As with tones and vowels, Tarok has a more elaborate system of nominal prefixes than the other members'; no stress/accent anywhere.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. (possible 2020s Kay Williamson Educational Foundation re-issue) The Yangkam language of Central Nigeria and its affinities. academia.edu, if it exists (cf. the 2023 re-issues of the sister Pe and Sur papers, academia.edu 102454393 etc.).
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Blench re-issued the Pe and Sur wordlist papers in 2023 with slightly expanded phonology sections; a parallel Yangkam re-issue could add a sentence on prosody. Existence not confirmed: academia.edu could not be reached by automated download, the Internet Archive's index for academia.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 2012. The Tarokoid languages of East-Central Nigeria. Unpublished manuscript, 65 pp. (Glottolog ref 311356; cited by the earlier scan as containing a Yangkam phonology sketch pp. 17-18).
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Only known longer treatment of Tarokoid after the 2004/2006 drafts; if any remark on Yangkam stress/accent exists in print it would be here. Likely repeats the two-tone statement, but unverified.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger M. 1998 field recordings of Yangkam (Tukur, 30 March 1998; Yuli/Tukur May 1996), taped per Blench 2006 p. 2; unpublished.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: The only primary audio of the language (ca. 100 elderly speakers in 1998, moribund); any future prosodic statement would have to come from these tapes or new fieldwork. Not a published source.
